etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English enforcen, from Old French enforcier, from Late Latin infortiāre, from in- + fortis (“strong”).

definitions.definition: To keep up, impose or bring into effect something, not necessarily by force. [from 17th c.]

quote.citation: 1929, Chiang Kai-shek, quoted in “Nationalist Notes,” Time, 11 February, 1929,[1]
quote.text: Our task is only half finished. It will be my duty to enforce the decisions of the conference and I hereby pledge myself to that end.

quote.citation: 2013 September 8, “The pulpit should be free of politics”, in Los Angeles Times:
quote.text: Far from needing to be repealed, the ban on politics in the pulpit ought to be enforced more aggressively.

definitions.definition: To give strength or force to; to affirm, to emphasize. [from 15th c.]
(obsolete, transitive) To strengthen (a castle, town etc.) with extra troops, fortifications etc. [14th–18th c.]
(obsolete, transitive) To intensify, make stronger, add force to. [14th–18th c.]
(obsolete, reflexive) To exert oneself, to try hard. [14th–17th c.]

quote.citation: 1470–1485 (date produced), Thomas Malory, “(please specify the chapter)”, in [Le Morte Darthur], book VII, [London:  […]  by William Caxton], published 31 July 1485, →OCLC; republished as H[einrich] Oskar Sommer, editor, Le Morte Darthur […], London: David Nutt, […], 1889, →OCLC:
quote.text: I pray you enforce youreselff at that justis that ye may be beste, for my love.(please add an English translation of this quotation)

definitions.definition: (obsolete) To compel, oblige (someone or something); to force. [from 16th c.]

quote.citation: 1594, Christopher Marlow[e], The Troublesome Raigne and Lamentable Death of Edward the Second, King of England: […], London:  […]  [Eliot’s Court Press] for Henry Bell, […], published 1622, →OCLC, (please specify the page):
quote.text: Sweete prince I come, these these thy amorous lines, / Might haue enforst me to haue swum from France, / And like Leander gaspt vpon the sande, / So thou wouldst smile and take me in thy armes.

quote.citation: 1624, Democritus Junior [pseudonym; Robert Burton], The Anatomy of Melancholy: […], 2nd edition, Oxford, Oxfordshire:  […]  John Lichfield and James Short, for Henry Cripps, →OCLC, partition I, section 2, member 4, subsection iv:
quote.text: Uladislaus the Second, King of Poland, and Peter Dunnius, Earl of Shrine […] had been hunting late, and were enforced to lodge in a poor cottage.

quote.citation: 1899, E. OE. Somerville, Martin Ross, Some Experiences of an Irish R.M., Great Uncle McCarthy:
quote.text: In a few minutes I was stealthily groping my way down my own staircase, with a box of matches in my hand, enforced by scientific curiosity, but none the less armed with a stick.

definitions.definition: (obsolete) To make or gain by force; to force.

quote.citation: 1590, Edmund Spenser, “Book I, Canto VIII”, in The Faerie Queene. […], London:  […]  [John Wolfe] for William Ponsonbie, →OCLC, page 106:
quote.text: Ne shame he thought to shonne so hideous might, / The ydle stroke, enforcing furious way, / Missing the marke of his misaymed sight / Did fall to ground  […]

definitions.definition: (obsolete) To put in motion or action by violence; to drive.

quote.citation: 1599 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Life of Henry the Fift”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act IV, scene vii]:

definitions.definition: (obsolete) To give force to; to strengthen; to invigorate; to energize.

quote.citation: 1796, Edmund Burke, “Letter I. On the Overtures of Peace.”, in Two Letters Addressed to a Member of the Present Parliament on the Proposals for Peace with the Regicide Directory of France, London:  […]  F[rancis] and C[harles] Rivington, […], published 20 October 1796, →OCLC, page 60:

definitions.definition: (obsolete) To urge; to ply hard; to lay much stress upon.

quote.citation: c. 1608–1609 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Tragedy of Coriolanus”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act III, scene ii]:
quote.text: In this point charge him home, that he affects / Tyrannical power: if he evade us there, / Enforce him with his envy to the people, / And that the spoil got on the Antiates / Was ne’er distributed.

quote.citation: 1594, Richard Hooker, “A Preface to Them that Seeke (as They Terme It) the Reformation of Lawes and Orders Ecclesiasticall, in the Church of England”, in J[ohn] S[penser], editor, Of the Lawes of Ecclesiastical Politie, […], 3rd edition, London:  […]  Will[iam] Stansby [for Matthew Lownes], published 1611, →OCLC, book I:
quote.text: But what argument are ye able to shew, whereby it was euer prooued by Caluin, that any one sentence of Scripture doth necessarily enforce these things, or the rest wherein your opinion concurreth with his against the orders of your owne Church?
